summary: Defines a Sieve extension for setting IMAP flags on messages at delivery. It supports both system flags and IMAP keywords, for example when a Sieve interpreter runs in a mail delivery agent. It is a standards-track specification.

eli5.summary: When mail arrives, this lets the sorting rules stick labels on it, like starred or read, so it shows up that way in your inbox.

questions: how to set imap flags with sieve
subtitle: Lets Sieve mail filters set, add, remove and test IMAP flags on a message as it is delivered.

tldr.problem: Sieve filters can file mail into folders, but they had no standard way to mark the message with IMAP flags such as \Flagged or custom keywords when it lands in the mailbox.
tldr.mechanism: The imap4flags extension adds three actions (setflag, addflag, removeflag), a hasflag test and a :flags argument for keep and fileinto, all working on a set of flags held in an internal variable or a named variable.
tldr.outcome: A script can now deliver a message already marked, for example as flagged or as a particular keyword, and can check flags it set earlier. It is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 5232 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 5228 (Sieve), RFC 3501 (IMAP) and RFC 5229 (variables).

sections.title: What the Extension Adds
sections.content:
RFC 5232 is an extension to the Sieve mail filtering language. It adds a new tagged argument, :flags, to keep and fileinto. That argument lists the IMAP flags to set when the message is delivered to the chosen mailbox. The RFC also adds actions to manipulate a list of flags and a test to check whether a flag is in a list.

The extension keeps an internal variable holding the default flags for a message delivered with keep, the implicit keep or fileinto when no :flags argument is given. If the Sieve variables extension is also supported, a script can use several named variables, each holding a set of flags.

The capability string is imap4flags. A conformant implementation MUST implement all three actions, the hasflag test and the :flags argument. Using an explicit variable name without the variables extension MUST cause an error.
sections.eli5: Sieve is a set of mail-sorting rules. This add-on lets the rules also put labels on mail and ask whether a label is already there.

sections.title: General Rules for Handling Flags
sections.content:
Several rules apply to every action, test and argument in the extension. Empty strings in a list of flags MUST be ignored. A single string with space-separated flag names is equivalent to a list of those flags, which makes it easy to join several lists. Multiple spaces count as one, and leading and trailing spaces MUST be ignored.

An interpreter SHOULD check each flag against the IMAP grammar, which does not allow non-ASCII characters in flag names. A flag that fails the check MUST be ignored. The extension also cannot set or clear the \Recent flag or any other special system flag that IMAP does not let clients set; such flags MUST be ignored.

Flag lists are case-insensitive sets. An action may reorder flags, change their case or drop duplicates, so scripts MUST NOT assume anything about ordering or case.
sections.eli5: Labels are just a pile of words, and the order and capital letters do not matter. Blank labels and labels that are not allowed are quietly thrown away.

sections.title: The Three Actions
sections.content:
All three actions work on a variable holding a set of flags. The variable name is optional; if it is left out, the action uses the internal variable, which is empty when the script starts.

  • setflag replaces any previously set flags.
  • addflag adds flags without replacing the old ones, so repeated uses are additive.
  • removeflag clears flags, and removing a flag that was never set is not an error.

For instance, two addflag actions adding \Deleted and \Answered give the same result as one action adding both in a list or in a single string. If keep or fileinto is used several times and duplicate message elimination happens, the last flag list value MUST win.
sections.eli5: Setflag wipes the labels and writes new ones. Addflag sticks on more labels. Removeflag peels a label off, and it does not mind if the label was not there.

sections.title: The hasflag Test
sections.content:
The hasflag test is true if any of the given variables matches any of the given flag names. The match type defaults to :is, and if the list of variables is left out, the internal variable is used.

The default comparator is i;ascii-casemap, the same case-insensitive comparison IMAP uses for flags. With the relational extension, the :count match type counts the distinct flags in a variable, and the count of a list of variables is the sum of the counts of its members. In the RFC's example, a variable holding A B satisfies :count "ge" 2.
sections.eli5: This is a question you ask about the labels: does this letter already have the label I am looking for?

sections.title: The :flags Argument and Other Actions
sections.content:
With :flags, the copy of the message filed into the mailbox has only the flags listed after the argument. Without it, keep and fileinto use the current value of the internal variable.

The interpreter MUST ignore any flag it cannot store permanently, and failing to store a flag MUST NOT be treated as a runtime failure of the script. So if a mailbox cannot hold flags, fileinto :flags "\\Deleted" "INBOX.From Boss" is the same as a plain fileinto. The RFC does not say how the interpreter sets the flags: it may act as an IMAP client or have direct access to the mail store.

The extension only touches the message currently being processed. It does not affect other messages generated as a side effect of an action or messages already in the store, and it does not change the implicit keep.
sections.eli5: When the helper files the letter, it puts on exactly the labels you listed. If a tray cannot hold labels, the letter is filed anyway without a fuss.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC's examples show the pieces working together. One script checks whether the sender is the boss, sets \Flagged in a variable, and files the message into a folder with that flag. Another adds $MDNRequired to a variable when a read-receipt header is present, then removes it for a particular mailing list before filing.

The extended example in Section 9 builds flags up in a variable called MyFlags. Messages over 1M get Big, mail from the boss also gets \Flagged, and mail from a named sender gets \Answered and $MDNSent. Each message is then filed with fileinto :flags "${MyFlags}".
sections.eli5: The examples show a helper who labels big letters, letters from the boss and letters from grandma differently, then files each one in the right tray.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC points to the security considerations of IMAP, Sieve and the Sieve variables extension. It notes that this extension intentionally does not allow setting IMAP flags on an arbitrary message in the IMAP message store, only on the message being delivered.

It is believed that the extension does not introduce any additional security concerns.
sections.eli5: The helper can only label the letter it is holding right now, not letters already sitting in your trays, so it cannot make a mess of old mail.
